description: A team from the Kushimoto Local Event, Japan. We enjoy building simulation and strategy games, and I’m excited to turn the trade-offs of real space mission design into something people can play, learn from, and replay. Looking forward to a great hackathon!
summary: Trade Space is a turn-based game in which students run a space agency and take a whole mission from concept to operations. In five phases (concept, spacecraft, launch booking, testing, operations) the player chooses orbits, instruments, rockets and tests under limits on mass, power, data, budget and schedule. Before confirming each phase, the player can fly the design 100 times in a forecast and see the chance of success and its weak points. Then event cards, many based on real cases such as Kepler's reaction wheel or a lunar lander on its side, hit the player and three rival agencies alike; who is hurt depends on what each one chose. A final scene flies all four missions, and the results explain why the player ranked where they did. There are three missions (a wildfire-watch CubeSat, a lunar south-pole ice rover, an icy-moon explorer at Jupiter), solo play against rule-based rivals or 2-4 players on one screen, and English and Japanese. Every number comes from NASA and other public sources and is linked in the game.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Trade Space makes the trade-offs of mission design visible. The player starts from an auto-plan that keeps cost and effort as low as possible and ignores risk. Each phase follows the same three steps.

1. Choose. Option cards show mass, power, data, cost and time, and what each option protects against. Gauges and a 3D mission view react at once.

2. Forecast. One forecast per phase flies the current design to the end 100 times. The player sees the chance of success, a score range, the most common failures, and how far the design has moved from the auto-plan.

3. Confirm. Event cards are drawn once and hit all four agencies. A card may be avoided, partly avoided, or taken in full, depending on earlier choices. Changing a past decision is possible but costs money and days.

After phase 5 the game flies the four missions side by side and then explains the result: where points were lost, what the winner did differently, and which decisions made the difference. "Same events, new design" lets the player try again against the same events.

WHY IT MATTERS

Students rarely see a mission from start to finish. Here a full mission takes about 15 minutes, failure is cheap, and every failure has a reason the player can read and act on. The intended lesson is that margin, testing and protection cost something, and that their value only shows when something goes wrong.

WHAT IS IN IT

- Three missions: Wildfire Watch CubeSat (beginner), Lunar South Pole Ice Rover (intermediate), Icy Moon Explorer at Jupiter (advanced).

- 47 event cards. Cards with a year are based on a real case, with the source linked.

- Solo against three rule-based agencies (cautious, balanced, bold), or 2-4 players taking turns on one screen. Nobody sees the others' choices until everyone has decided.

- A guide for first-time players, optional hints, and a practice mode with unlimited forecasts.

- A browsable library of all event cards and a glossary.

- English and Japanese.

HOW IT IS BUILT

- React, TypeScript and Vite. The 3D views use three.js. Sound effects are synthesised with the Web Audio API.

- It runs entirely in the browser. There is no server, no account, and no AI model at run time. Rivals follow fixed rules.

- The simulation is seeded, so the same seed gives the same events for everyone and forecasts can be compared fairly.

- Every value in the game data records its source. A check script fails if a value cites an unknown source.

- The forecast branch map and the seeded random-number generator were ported from the author's own earlier, unpublished simulator (TACTICA DSS).

NASA DATA IN THE GAME

- The fire dots on the globe are real 2024 detections from NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1).

- Solar-storm chances are counted from NASA DONKI.

- Spacecraft parts and limits follow NASA's State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report and CubeSat 101; the lunar and Jupiter missions follow public VIPER and Europa Clipper documents.

- The Earth uses NASA's Blue Marble image. Jupiter and the Moon are drawn in code and are not to scale.

- The game uses 52 NASA sources and 20 others. The complete list, with links, is in the repository: https://github.com/kaisakut/space-mission-design-game/blob/main/src/data/sources.ts

We acknowledge the use of data and/or imagery from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) (https://earthdata.nasa.gov/firms), part of NASA's Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS).

USE OF AI

The code, the game text and its Japanese translation, the icons (drawn as code) and the research for the game data were produced with an AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) under the team's direction. The team decided what the game should teach and how it plays, made the design decisions at each step, and reviewed the results by playing the game. Sources were opened and compared with the values in the game. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used. This is also stated in the repository README.
